issues.subcategory: results based on dummy/randomized data
issues.description: The manuscript explicitly states that the results were generated from a randomized Qualtrics dummy dataset rather than actual participant data. Consequently, all inferential statistics, conclusions, and claims about empirical support are not interpretable as study findings. This is a critical validity problem unless the manuscript is clearly framed only as a preregistration/protocol rather than an empirical report.
issues.quote: Results were written using randomized dataset produced by Qualtrics to simulate what these sections will look like after data collection. These will be updated following the data collection.

issues.subcategory: claims data collection completed despite dummy data
issues.description: The manuscript simultaneously states that data collection was completed before analyses and that methods/results are based on randomized Qualtrics data to be updated after data collection. These statements are contradictory and make it impossible to determine whether the reported analyses are preregistered mock analyses or post-data empirical analyses.
issues.quote: All measures, manipulations, exclusions conducted for this investigation are reported, all studies were pre-registered with power analyses reported in the supplementary, and data collection was completed before analyses.

issues.subcategory: abstract reports simulated findings as empirical results
issues.description: The abstract presents dummy-data results as if they were empirical findings, including claims of support or lack of support for hypotheses. This is misleading because the dataset is randomized and not collected from participants.
issues.quote: We generated a dummy set of samples in the Qualtrics survey (N = 1000) and found no empirical support for the effect of analytical reasoning on the identifiable victim effect. To extend the replication, we added the “perceived impact of donation” as a factor that is believed to be linked with the identifiable victim effect. Results have supported the hypothesis that people have a lower rating of perceived impact of donation when they faced an identifiable victim or an identifiable victim provided with victim statistics.

issues.subcategory: not a close replication due to major design changes
issues.description: The study is described as a close to very close replication, but multiple central features differ from the original: online MTurk rather than laboratory/student center recruitment, hypothetical rather than real donation, no earned endowment, updated victim stimuli, merged Studies 1 and 3, added joint-condition intervention, and added measures. These changes alter the psychological context, incentive compatibility, and construct being measured, weakening claims of close replication.
issues.quote: In this replication, we merged Studies 1 and 3 into one single experiment... The intervention of learning about the effect would also be applied to the joint condition... Imaginary donation Participants are required to indicate how much they would donate from $0 to $5... instead of donating the money to Save the Children after signing a charity request letter.

issues.subcategory: hypothetical donation substitutes for real charitable behavior
issues.description: The original dependent variable involved donating real money received by participants. The replication uses an imaginary donation amount. Hypothetical willingness to donate may not capture actual costly helping behavior and is vulnerable to demand characteristics and social desirability, undermining construct validity and comparability to the target study.
issues.quote: Imaginary donation Participants are required to indicate how much they would donate from $0 to $5 to the corresponding victim(s) instead of donating the money to Save the Children after signing a charity request letter.

issues.subcategory: removal of earned endowment changes incentive structure
issues.description: The original participants donated from money they had just received, whereas the replication removes the presurvey/endowment. This changes whether participants perceive the money as a windfall, earned income, or purely hypothetical, and may affect donation behavior and emotional engagement.
issues.quote: No reward acquired from a pre-survey  Participants will not conduct an irrelevant survey prior to the experiment to earn $5 for the donation

issues.subcategory: combining Study 1 and Study 3 introduces confounding
issues.description: The replication merges two originally separate studies and applies the explicit intervention to the joint condition. This creates a factorial structure not present in the target studies and confounds replication of the original effects with new design elements. The joint condition is not directly comparable to either original Study 1 or Study 3.
issues.quote: In this replication, we merged Studies 1 and 3 into one single experiment... The intervention of learning about the effect would also be applied to the joint condition to reveal a more comprehensive comparison between the explicit and implicit settings.

issues.subcategory: incorrect or inappropriate effect-size metric for interaction
issues.description: The manuscript reports Cohen’s d for the interaction effect in the original 2×2 ANOVA. Cohen’s d is not generally the appropriate effect-size measure for a factorial interaction unless a specific contrast or difference-in-differences is defined. The method for deriving d and its confidence interval is not described, making the power analysis and replication evaluation questionable.
issues.quote: The interaction effect was d = 0.41, 95% CI [0.05, 0.77] when explicit learning was adopted to debias the identifiable victim effect.

issues.subcategory: power analysis based on inappropriate effect and test
issues.description: The power analysis uses Cohen’s d = -0.36 for the intervention main effect from the original study to justify N = 314, but the replication’s primary design is a 2×3 ANOVA with interaction hypotheses and post-hoc contrasts. Power for the focal interaction and specific planned contrasts should be calculated for the actual design, including allocation across six cells. Using a main-effect d from a different design may substantially misestimate required sample size.
issues.quote: Given the smallest effect size regarding the effect of intervention (learning identifiable victim effect or not) on donation was found in the original study with Cohens’d = -0.36, the corresponding sample size to detect such effect was 314.

issues.subcategory: sample-size justification inconsistent with reported N
issues.description: The manuscript states that the required sample size was 314 but uses N = 1000 dummy responses, without explaining the actual intended sample size, whether N = 1000 is planned, or whether the study is overpowered relative to the stated calculation. The sample-size rationale is incomplete and inconsistent with the reported design.
issues.quote: A total of 1000 responses were generated from the Qualtrics for pre-registration... the corresponding sample size to detect such effect was 314.

issues.subcategory: participant source and compensation unspecified
issues.description: Critical details about recruitment, eligibility, location, compensation, and actual sampling frame are missing or inconsistent. The table says geographic origin and compensation are not specified, while another section says MTurk workers will be recruited. These details are essential for evaluating sample quality, generalizability, and comparability to the original study.
issues.quote: Geographic origin | US American | Not specified | Not specified... Compensation | US$5 | Not specified | Not specified

issues.subcategory: MTurk platform named inconsistently
issues.description: The manuscript refers to the recruitment platform as 'Mechanical Amazon Turk' rather than Amazon Mechanical Turk and elsewhere says the sample origin is not specified. This suggests imprecise or incomplete reporting of recruitment procedures.
issues.quote: Participants will conduct an online survey in Qualtrics on the Mechanical Amazon Turk platform

issues.subcategory: sample age distribution implausible and unaddressed
issues.description: The generated sample has a mean age of 67.8, SD = 30.1, and range 18–120, which is implausible for typical MTurk samples and likely reflects dummy/random data. If reported as real data, this would raise severe data-quality concerns. Even as dummy data, it should not be used to characterize the planned sample.
issues.quote: A total of 1000 responses were generated from the Qualtrics for pre-registration (Mage = 67.80, SD=30.10; 471 females and 529 males).

issues.subcategory: no exclusion or data-quality criteria
issues.description: The manuscript states that no samples were excluded but does not specify attention checks, duplicate screening, bot detection, comprehension checks, location/IP restrictions, or preregistered exclusion rules. For online MTurk research, these procedures are important to ensure valid responses.
issues.quote: There was no exclusion of samples in this study.

issues.subcategory: randomization procedure insufficiently described
issues.description: The manuscript states that participants will be assigned randomly but provides no details on the randomization algorithm, allocation ratio, blocking, Qualtrics randomizer settings, or whether randomization occurred before exclusions. This limits reproducibility and evaluation of internal validity.
issues.quote: Participants will be assigned randomly to the intervention and identifiability conditions.

issues.subcategory: lack of manipulation checks
issues.description: The deliberative-thinking intervention is assumed to work by teaching participants about the identifiable victim effect, but the manuscript does not report checks that participants read, understood, or engaged in deliberative/analytical thinking. Without manipulation checks, null effects cannot be interpreted as failure of the theoretical effect rather than failure of the manipulation.
issues.quote: Participants under manipulation were taught about the identifiable victim effect before donating to the victims.

issues.subcategory: intervention operationalization may induce demand characteristics
issues.description: Explicitly teaching participants about the identifiable victim effect before asking them to donate may cue the expected behavior and produce compliance or reactance rather than genuine deliberative thinking. The manuscript does not address demand characteristics or include controls to distinguish deliberation from demand awareness.
issues.quote: one group learning about the identifiable victim effect from previous research while another served as a control group

issues.subcategory: perceived impact hypothesis conflicts with reported abstract claim
issues.description: The extension hypothesis predicts that identifiable victims elicit higher perceived impact than statistical victims, but the abstract claims that people had lower perceived impact when facing an identifiable victim or identifiable victim with statistics. This contradiction undermines conceptual clarity and interpretation.
issues.quote: It is hypothesized that people generally perceive a stronger impact of donation towards an identified victim than unidentified statistical victims.

issues.subcategory: extension result described inconsistently
issues.description: The results section says statistical victims had higher perceived impact than the joint condition, whereas the abstract says lower perceived impact occurred for identifiable or identifiable-with-statistics victims. The hypothesis table says identifiable victims should elicit higher perceived impact than statistical victims. These inconsistent directional statements make the extension unclear.
issues.quote: This suggested that participants who faced a statistical victim (M=3.12, SD=1.43) had a higher rating of perceived impact of their donation to help the victims than they faced an identifiable victim provided with victim statistics (M=2.85, SD=1.34).

issues.subcategory: Bonferroni post-hoc interpretation inconsistent with confidence intervals
issues.description: Several post-hoc tests report statistically significant Bonferroni-adjusted p-values while the reported confidence intervals for d include zero, e.g., p = .049 with d CI [-0.05, 0.20] and p = .041 with d CI [-0.07, 0.23]. This is internally inconsistent unless the confidence intervals are not aligned with the adjusted tests or are incorrectly calculated/reported. It may indicate statistical reporting errors.

issues.subcategory: effect size sign inconsistent with t statistic
issues.description: In Table 10, the t statistic for Identifiable vs Statistical is negative, but Cohen’s d is positive. The direction of the contrast is unclear and inconsistent, complicating interpretation of which group donated more.

issues.subcategory: implausibly tiny Cohen's d for mean difference
issues.description: The reported Cohen’s d for the identifiable vs statistical donation comparison is d = 0.076 despite means of 2.54 versus 2.24 and SDs around 1.7, which would imply d around 0.17–0.18, not 0.076. This suggests a calculation or reporting error, perhaps confusing standardized mean difference with another effect-size metric.
issues.quote: participants who faced an identifiable victim (M=2.54, SD=1.76) tended to donate more than those who faced the statistical victims (M=2.24, SD=1.67).

issues.subcategory: post-hoc contrast likely uses inappropriate independent-samples t-test
issues.description: The contrast compares the identifiable/no-intervention cell with the combination of five other cells using t(998), apparently treating the two groups as independent groups of sizes 175 and 825. However, this contrast follows from a factorial ANOVA and should be specified as a planned contrast within the ANOVA/general linear model with appropriate contrast weights, not an ad hoc pooled t-test after inspecting interaction significance. The analysis also changes the original contrast by adding joint conditions.
issues.quote: we also conducted a t-test to study if the mean of identifiable/no intervention condition is different from the mean of combining other five conditions on donation.

issues.subcategory: conditional post-hoc testing based on significance
issues.description: The analysis plan conducts post-hoc tests only if omnibus or interaction effects are significant. Such gatekeeping can be acceptable if preregistered, but it increases analytic complexity and may obscure the primary confirmatory tests. The manuscript does not clearly distinguish confirmatory planned contrasts from exploratory follow-ups.
issues.quote: Post-hoc contrast test   (Note: we conduct the test only if the interaction effect is significant)

issues.subcategory: ANOVA may be inappropriate for bounded ordinal/count-like donation outcome
issues.description: Donation ranges from $0 to $5 and in the original study represented discrete dollar amounts. A two-way ANOVA assumes approximately continuous normally distributed residuals and homoscedasticity. The original also used ordered probit regression, but the replication omits it without justification. For bounded, potentially ordinal/censored donation data, ordered, binomial, Tobit, or robust models may be more appropriate or at least sensitivity analyses should be reported.
issues.quote: Ordered probit regression... This test would not be conducted in the replication

issues.subcategory: assumption checks missing for ANOVA and correlations
issues.description: The manuscript relies on ANOVA and Pearson correlations but does not report checks of normality, homogeneity of variance, independence, outliers, linearity, or robustness. This is particularly important for bounded donation amounts and Likert-type affect measures.
issues.quote: We conducted the data analysis with JAMOVI for statistical testing and R for calculation of 95%CI given that such function is not available for ANOVA testing in JAMOVI.

issues.subcategory: multiple comparisons not controlled comprehensively
issues.description: The manuscript analyzes multiple outcomes: donation, aggregated feelings, six segregated feelings, multiple main effects/interactions, post-hoc comparisons, and six correlations. Bonferroni adjustment is mentioned for some pairwise tests, but there is no clear familywise or false-discovery-rate correction across the many tests. This inflates Type I error, particularly for the extension finding with p = .045.
issues.quote: Segregated feelings include being upsetting, being touched, being sympathetic, moral responsibility, donation appropriateness, and perceived impact of donation (extension)

issues.subcategory: aggregation of heterogeneous affective and moral items unjustified
issues.description: The manuscript combines upset, touched, sympathy, moral responsibility, donation appropriateness, and possibly perceived impact into an aggregated feelings index. These variables reflect distinct constructs—emotion, moral obligation, perceived appropriateness, and efficacy—and should not be aggregated without psychometric justification such as reliability, factor structure, and preregistered scoring.
issues.quote: Note: combine segregated feelings into one aggregated feeling

issues.subcategory: extension measure conflated with affective feelings
issues.description: Perceived impact of donation is an efficacy/cognitive appraisal construct, not an affective feeling. The manuscript includes it among segregated feelings while also calling it an extension, which creates construct confusion and may distort the aggregated feeling measure if included.
issues.quote: Segregated feelings include being upsetting, being touched, being sympathetic, moral responsibility, donation appropriateness, and perceived impact of donation (extension)

issues.subcategory: measurement items and scales not reported in manuscript
issues.description: The manuscript does not provide exact wording, response scales, anchors, timing, or scoring for donation, affective reactions, moral responsibility, donation appropriateness, or perceived impact. Referring readers to supplementary materials is helpful but insufficient for evaluating and replicating the key measures from the manuscript itself.
issues.quote: After the donation, they had to fill up a questionnaire for different affective reactions... These items included the feeling of being upset, being touched, being sympathetic, moral responsibility, and the appropriateness of donation to help the victims.

issues.subcategory: stimuli insufficiently specified
issues.description: The replication says victim information will be updated from Save the Children but does not include the exact text, victim identity, statistics, date, charity context, or comparability checks. Stimulus content can substantially affect sympathy and donations, so insufficient specification limits reproducibility and interpretation.
issues.quote: We will present the participants with the most updated victim information retrieved from the website of Save the Children given that those used in the original study was dated two decades ago.

issues.subcategory: updated stimuli may alter target effect
issues.description: Using updated victim information may change salience, vividness, severity, cultural context, credibility, and emotional impact relative to the original. Without pretesting equivalence, differences in outcomes may reflect stimulus differences rather than replication success/failure.
issues.quote: Updated victim information  We will present the participants with the most updated victim information retrieved from the website of Save the Children

issues.subcategory: correlational affect-donation analyses described predictively
issues.description: The manuscript uses correlations between feelings and donation to examine whether affective feelings 'predict' donation. Because feelings and donations are measured in the same experimental session and may be mutually influenced or jointly caused by condition, causal or directional interpretation is not warranted.
issues.quote: We conducted a correlation between aggregated feelings and donation to examine whether affective feelings predict donation.

issues.subcategory: mediation implication without mediation analysis
issues.description: The introduction frames perceived impact as linked to or potentially mediating the identifiable victim effect, but the analysis only tests mean differences by condition. No mediation model, temporal ordering, or assumptions are specified, so claims about perceived impact explaining donation behavior are unsupported.
issues.quote: Yet, there were mixed findings regarding the mediation effect of perceived impact on the identifiable victim effect.

issues.subcategory: table numbering errors
issues.description: The manuscript references Table 7 as the replication classification table, but the actual classification table is labeled Table 6, and later Table 7 is descriptive statistics. Such numbering errors reduce clarity and may signal version-control problems.
issues.quote: Table 7 summarizes the current replication as a "close to very close replication".

issues.subcategory: duplicate columns in Table 4
issues.description: Table 4 appears to contain duplicate replication columns, with the same values repeated twice. This creates confusion about whether there are multiple replication samples or a formatting error.
issues.quote: Sample size | Study 1: 121 Study 3: 159 | 1000 | 1000

issues.subcategory: ANOVA degrees of freedom imply full N but no missing-data reporting
issues.description: All ANOVA residual df are reported as 994 for a 2×3 design, implying complete data from all 1000 cases. However, the manuscript does not report whether any participants failed to answer measures, how missing responses were handled, or whether analyses used listwise deletion. This is especially important for online surveys.
issues.quote: Residual | 994

issues.subcategory: missing data handling absent
issues.description: The manuscript does not describe missing data, incomplete survey responses, attrition, nonresponse to donation or affect measures, or the analytic handling of such cases. Online survey studies commonly have partial completions, and missingness can bias results if not handled transparently.
issues.quote: There was no exclusion of samples in this study.

issues.subcategory: no blinding or demand-minimization procedures reported
issues.description: The study involves explicit teaching about a bias followed by a donation decision. The manuscript does not describe any blinding of participants to hypotheses, cover story, suspicion probes, or steps to reduce experimenter/participant expectancy effects. This matters because the manipulation may reveal the study purpose.
issues.quote: participants under manipulation were taught about the identifiable victim effect before donating to the victims

issues.subcategory: online MTurk sample differs from original student-center sample
issues.description: The original study recruited people in a university student center in Pennsylvania, whereas the replication plans online MTurk workers. Differences in demographics, socioeconomic status, prior exposure to psychology tasks, donation norms, and attention may limit comparability and generalizability. The manuscript lists this as a deviation but does not adequately discuss implications.
issues.quote: MTurk workers as participants We will recruit participants on the Mechanical Amazon Turk platform while the original study recruited participants sitting inside the school centre of a university in Pennsylvania

issues.subcategory: cell sizes unequal and unexplained
issues.description: Reported cell sizes vary from 159 to 175 despite random assignment to six conditions. Unequal cell sizes may arise by chance or survey randomizer settings, but the manuscript does not explain allocation ratios or whether imbalance reflects attrition or missingness.

issues.subcategory: omnibus interaction not followed by appropriate simple effects
issues.description: The manuscript reports a significant identifiability × intervention interaction on donation but does not test the theoretically relevant simple effects: intervention within identifiable victims, intervention within statistical victims, and joint vs identifiable no-intervention comparisons. Instead, it uses a broad contrast of one cell versus all other cells, which does not directly test Hypotheses 3 and 4.
issues.quote: Given the significant interaction effect, we also conducted a t-test to study if the mean of identifiable/no intervention condition is different from the mean of combining other five conditions on donation.

issues.subcategory: implicit learning terminology questionable
issues.description: The manuscript describes the joint condition as 'implicitly learning about the identifiable victim effect,' but participants are not necessarily learning the effect; they are exposed to both identifiable and statistical information. This conflates implicit deliberation/comparison with learning and may mislabel the manipulation.
issues.quote: participants implicitly learning about the effect would not be presented with such information but with the provision of victim statistics in the identifiable victim condition.

issues.subcategory: overgeneralized normative claim about resource allocation
issues.description: The introduction states that identifiable-victim giving reflects inefficiency and unfairness in valuing life, but this normative claim is not directly tested and may depend on charitable context, marginal effectiveness, and donor goals. It risks overstating the conceptual implications of the phenomenon.
issues.quote: The inconsistent prosocial motivation not only demonstrates human sense of unfairness in valuing life, but also highlights the lack of efficiency in resource allocation when asserts are accumulated on a single victim instead of dispersing to a greater population to benefit the society as a whole.

issues.subcategory: reported p thresholds incomplete for original statistics
issues.description: Original findings are reported only as p < .05 or p < .01, while replication results use exact p-values. This limits quantitative comparison and may affect replication evaluation, especially when original F values and dfs allow exact p-values to be computed.
issues.quote: F | p | ηp2... Identifiability | ... 6.75 | <.05* | .06

issues.subcategory: pre-registration details incomplete in manuscript
issues.description: Although an OSF link is provided, the manuscript does not summarize key preregistered elements: exact primary outcomes, primary tests, exclusion criteria, stopping rule, sample-size target, deviations, and whether analyses reported here match the preregistration. The 'OSF pre-registration review' field is blank.
issues.quote: OSF pre-registration review:.

issues.subcategory: unclear confirmatory versus exploratory status of extension and added conditions
issues.description: The study adds perceived impact, measures feelings in the joint condition, and applies intervention to joint conditions. It is not clear which analyses are confirmatory preregistered replication tests versus exploratory extensions. This ambiguity increases risk of selective interpretation.
issues.quote: We will measure affective feelings in the Joint condition which was not measured in the original study. We will also add an extension of the “perceived impact of donation” into the scale.

issues.subcategory: description of replication effect target mismatched to study goals
issues.description: The evaluation criteria say the replication effect will be compared to the original main effect of identifiability d = 0.48, but the central stated goal is the effect of deliberative thinking on the identifiable victim effect, which is primarily an interaction or debiasing contrast. The target effect for replication evaluation is therefore unclear.
issues.quote: We aim to study the effect of deliberative thinking on identifiable victim effect by comparing the replication effect with the original effect (d = 0.48, 95% CI [0.11, 0.84])

issues.subcategory: partial eta-squared confidence intervals reported without method
issues.description: The manuscript reports confidence intervals for partial eta-squared but does not specify calculation method, software/package, or whether intervals are one-sided/lower-bound constrained. Several intervals start at 0.00 despite significant effects, which may be technically possible but requires explanation for interpretation.

issues.subcategory: no demographic covariates or sample characteristics beyond age/gender
issues.description: The manuscript provides minimal demographic information and omits income, education, nationality, ethnicity, religion, prior charitable giving, or familiarity with Save the Children. These variables may affect donation decisions and are relevant for sample characterization and generalizability, even if not used as covariates.
issues.quote: Gender | Not specified | 529 males, 471 females... Average age (years) | Not specified | 67.8 | 67.8

issues.subcategory: charity credibility and real donation implementation unclear
issues.description: Because the donation is imaginary, it is unclear whether participants believe any donation will occur, whether the charity is named, or whether there is deception. The original involved a Save the Children request, which likely influenced realism and trust. The replication does not sufficiently specify how credibility and realism are maintained.
issues.quote: Participants are required to indicate how much they would donate from $0 to $5 to the corresponding victim(s) instead of donating the money to Save the Children after signing a charity request letter.

issues.subcategory: correlation analyses underpowered by condition not discussed despite total N large
issues.description: Although total N is 1000, within-condition correlations are based on approximately 159–175 participants per cell. The manuscript does not report power or precision for these correlations, despite interpreting null correlations across conditions.
issues.quote: correlation between aggregated feelings and donation across six different conditions

issues.subcategory: misalignment between identifiable victim effect and joint condition interpretation
issues.description: The identifiable victim effect is defined as greater helping for a single identified victim compared to statistical victims. The joint condition includes both an identifiable victim and statistics, which may not represent a simple level of identifiability but a qualitatively different informational context involving joint evaluation, numeracy, and comparison. Treating it as a third level of identifiability may obscure interpretation.
issues.quote: We embedded Studies 1 and 3 of Small et al. (2007) into a single between-subject design with identifiability and intervention as the independent variables

issues.subcategory: main-effect interpretation inappropriate in presence of interaction
issues.description: The results emphasize a main effect of identifiability on donation even though the identifiability × intervention interaction is significant. Main effects in the presence of interactions can be misleading and should be interpreted cautiously with simple effects or planned contrasts.
issues.quote: Results from Table 9 showed that no significant effect was found on intervention but the identifiability and the interaction effect of identifiability and intervention was supported.

issues.subcategory: post-hoc perceived impact conclusion does not match stated extension hypothesis
issues.description: The extension hypothesis predicts identifiable victim > statistical victims in perceived impact. The only significant post-hoc comparison is statistical > joint, while identifiable vs statistical is nonsignificant. Thus the stated extension hypothesis is not supported, but the abstract claims support.

issues.subcategory: no discussion section provided despite requested interpretation
issues.description: The manuscript includes no substantive discussion interpreting limitations, deviations, dummy-data status, generalizability, or implications. Without a discussion, readers cannot evaluate how the authors qualify their claims or address methodological constraints.
issues.quote: References

issues.subcategory: control condition content insufficiently described
issues.description: The control condition is described only as not learning about the identifiable victim effect. It is unclear whether it receives equivalent reading time, cognitive load, informational content, or neutral text. Without an active control, effects may reflect time, attention, priming, or information exposure rather than deliberative thinking.
issues.quote: one group learning about the identifiable victim effect from previous research while another served as a control group

issues.subcategory: original Study 3 ANOVA reporting incomplete
issues.description: Table 2 reports Study 3 df1 = 2 but df2 = N/A despite N = 159; df2 could likely be inferred. Incomplete reporting impairs effect-size verification and comparison with the replication.
issues.quote: Identifiability Identifiable victim | 2.38 | N/A | 2 | N/A | 5.67 | <.01** | .07

issues.subcategory: donation recipient ambiguous in joint condition
issues.description: In the joint condition, participants receive both identifiable and statistical victim information, but it is unclear whether the donation amount is intended for the identifiable victim, statistical victims, both, or the charity generally. This ambiguity affects interpretation of donation as helping an identifiable versus statistical target.
issues.quote: The third group was considered as a joint condition provided with both statistical and identifiable victim information. The victim statistics was believed to eliminate the identifiable victim effect implicitly in the joint condition as reflected in the donation towards the identifiable victim.

issues.subcategory: timing/order of measures not fully specified
issues.description: The timing of intervention, victim information, donation decision, and affect measures is described only generally. Exact order matters because measuring feelings before donation could influence donation, while measuring after donation could reflect justification of the choice.
issues.quote: After the donation, they had to fill up a questionnaire for different affective reactions they experienced which may influence their choice of donation.

issues.subcategory: possible order and carryover effects in merged design not addressed
issues.description: Combining identifiable and statistical information in a joint condition introduces possible order effects depending on which information appears first. The manuscript does not state whether order is fixed or randomized, or how order effects will be handled.
issues.quote: provided with both statistical and identifiable victim information
